title: A personal story for a new big brother or sister
summary: A gentle story that helps a young child get ready for a new baby, with them as the proud big brother or sister.
why_it_helps: A new baby changes everything a small child knows about their place in the family. Seeing themselves in a story, being needed and still loved, gives them words for big feelings and something positive to look forward to. Reading it together before the birth, and again after, lets them practise the change somewhere safe.
tips:
Read it a few weeks before the baby arrives, then again in the first week home.
Pause on the pages about feelings and ask how they think the character feels.
Give them a real job that matches one in the story, like choosing the baby's socks.
sample_story:
{name} had a secret job. Mummy's tummy was getting bigger and bigger, and everyone said {name} was going to be a big sibling.

"What does a big sibling do?" asked {name}.

"They sing the best songs," said Daddy. "They know where the teddies live. And they give the gentlest cuddles."

When the baby came home, she was very small and very loud. Sometimes {name} felt a bit cross that everyone looked at the baby. That was OK. Grown-ups feel cross sometimes too.

But when the baby cried, {name} sang the teddy song. The baby went quiet and looked right at {name}.

"She knows you," whispered Mummy. "You're her big sibling."

{name} smiled. It was the best job in the whole house.

title: A personal story for a child starting nursery
summary: A short, reassuring story about a first day at nursery, where the child is the hero and the grown-up always comes back.
why_it_helps: Separation is one of the first big challenges for toddlers. A story that shows the whole day, including the moment the grown-up comes back, makes the routine predictable. Predictable feels safe, and safe children settle faster.
tips:
Use the real names of the nursery and a key person if you know them.
Read it in the days before starting, not just the night before.
Keep the goodbye in real life short and the same every day, just like the story.
sample_story:
Today {name} is going to nursery.

{name} has a bag with a water bottle and a spare jumper. At the door, Mummy gives {name} one big hug and one kiss on the nose.

"I always come back," says Mummy.

Inside there are blocks to build and paint to splash. There is a sandpit with a yellow digger. {name} misses Mummy a little bit, and Jo the nursery teacher gives {name} a cuddle.

After lunch it is story time. After story time it is outside time. After outside time, the door opens.

It's Mummy! She came back, just like she said.

"What did you do today?" she asks.

"I used the digger," says {name}. "Can I go again tomorrow?"

title: A personal story for a child starting Reception
summary: A confidence-building story about the first day of school, from putting on the new uniform to coming home with news to share.
why_it_helps: Starting school brings lots of new things at once: a uniform, a bigger building, new children and new rules. Walking through the day in a story, with themselves at the centre, turns unknowns into a plan. Children who know what to expect use their energy for learning, not worrying.
tips:
Add the real details: the school name, the teacher, the colour of the jumper.
Ask what they think they might play at break time.
Read it again at the end of the first week and talk about what was the same and what was different.
sample_story:
{name}'s new jumper was blue and a little bit too big. "You'll grow into it," said Grandad.

At the school gate there were lots of children and lots of grown-ups. {name}'s tummy felt fluttery, like butterflies were having a party.

Mrs Patel had a kind voice. She showed {name} a peg with {name}'s name on it. "This is your peg," she said. "It's here every day."

{name} painted a rocket. At lunch there was pasta. At playtime a girl called Ruby asked if {name} wanted to be the captain.

At home time, Grandad was waiting.

"How was it?" he asked.

"The butterflies flew away," said {name}. "And I'm a captain now."

title: A personal story for a child moving house
summary: A comforting story about moving to a new home, packing up favourite things and finding they all come too.
why_it_helps: Young children often think that when things go into boxes, they are gone. A story that shows their favourite things being packed, travelling and unpacked again makes the move feel solid. It also gives them a way to say goodbye to the old house.
tips:
Let them pack one special box themselves and mark it with a sticker.
Take a photo of their old bedroom to look at together later.
Set up their bed and favourite toys first in the new house, just like the story.
sample_story:
Everything in {name}'s house was going into boxes. The pans went into a box. The books went into a box. Even the cushions went into a box!

"Is Bunny going in a box?" asked {name}.

"Bunny can ride with you," said Dad. "And you can pack your own special box."

{name} said goodbye to the old garden and the old stairs and the tree by the window.

The big van drove to the new house. It had a red door and stairs that went round a corner.

One by one, the boxes opened. Out came the books. Out came the cushions. Out came {name}'s special box, with the dinosaur lamp on top.

That night, {name} and Bunny looked at the new ceiling.

"Everything came with us," said {name}. "This is home now."

title: A personal story for a toddler learning to use the potty
summary: An encouraging story about learning to use the potty, where accidents are normal and every try counts.
why_it_helps: Potty learning goes better when children feel in charge and unworried. A story where they are the one deciding, trying and sometimes getting it wrong takes the pressure off. It also gives parents simple, kind words to use on the tricky days.
tips:
Keep the potty somewhere they can see it while you read.
Celebrate tries, not just successes, the same way the story does.
If they have an accident, use the same calm words as the story.
sample_story:
{name} has a new potty. It is green, like a frog.

"When your tummy feels a wriggle, you can sit on the potty," says Mama.

The first time, nothing happens. "Good trying!" says Mama.

The second time, {name} is busy playing with the train and forgets. Oops! That's OK. Everyone forgets when they're learning.

The third time, {name} feels the wriggle, runs to the frog potty and sits down.

Tinkle tinkle!

"You did it!" says Mama. {name} does a happy dance. Mama does a happy dance too.

Now {name} knows what to do when the wriggle comes. Frog potty, here I come!

title: A personal story for a child's first dentist visit
summary: A friendly story about visiting the dentist, from the big chair that goes up and down to counting teeth.
why_it_helps: The dentist has bright lights, strange tools and a chair that moves, which can all feel scary when you don't know what's coming. A story that explains each step, with your child bravely doing it, turns the visit into something familiar before they arrive.
tips:
Play dentists with a toy, counting its teeth with a spoon.
Read it in the week before the appointment.
Tell the dentist your child has a story about the visit. Many will play along.
sample_story:
Today {name} is going to visit the tooth doctor. Her name is Dr Sam.

Dr Sam has a special chair. It goes up, up, up, and then it tips back like a rocket getting ready to fly.

"Can you open wide like a lion?" asks Dr Sam. {name} opens wide. ROAR!

Dr Sam has a little mirror on a stick. She counts {name}'s teeth. "One, two, three... twenty! What strong teeth."

The light is bright, so {name} wears cool sunglasses.

"All done," says Dr Sam. "You were a super brave lion."

On the way out, {name} gets a sticker of a tooth with a smiley face. {name} can't wait to show everyone.

title: A personal story for a child going into hospital
summary: A calm, honest story for a child with a hospital stay or operation coming up, focused on the people who help and going home again.
why_it_helps: Hospitals are full of unfamiliar sights and sounds. Children cope better when they are told honestly what will happen, in a way that fits their age. A story about their own visit, ending with going home, gives them something to hold on to. Ask your child's hospital team what to include, as many have play specialists who can help.
tips:
Check the details with the hospital, such as whether a grown-up can stay overnight.
Pack a comfort toy and put it in the story too.
Keep the language simple and honest. Avoid promising it won't hurt.
sample_story:
{name} is going to the hospital so the doctors can help make {name}'s tummy better.

At the hospital, everyone wears a name badge. A nurse called Ben gives {name} a bracelet with {name}'s name on it. "Now everyone knows who you are," he says.

{name} has a bed with buttons that make it go up and down. Teddy has his own spot on the pillow.

Sometimes there are beeps and sometimes there are things that feel strange. When that happens, {name} holds Mum's hand and squeezes three times. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. That means "I love you."

The doctors do their job. {name} has a long sleep.

And then, one morning, the nurse says the best words of all.

"Time to go home, {name}."

title: A personal story for a child whose grandparent lives far away
summary: A warm story that keeps a faraway grandparent close, with video calls, letters and plans for the next visit.
why_it_helps: When family live far away, young children can find it hard to feel close to them between visits. A story that puts the grandparent and child together, and shows the ways they stay in touch, makes the relationship real every time it's read. It's also a lovely book for the grandparent to read on a video call.
tips:
Use the name your child really calls their grandparent.
Read it together on a video call with the grandparent.
Add a real memory from the last visit.
sample_story:
{name}'s Nana lives far, far away, over the sea.

Nana can't come for tea on Tuesdays. But on Sundays, Nana's face pops up on the tablet.

"Hello, my sunshine!" says Nana. {name} shows Nana a wobbly tooth and a drawing of a whale.

Sometimes a letter comes in the post with Nana's curly writing and a sticker inside.

At night, {name} looks at the moon. "Nana can see the moon too," says Dad. "It's the same moon."

{name} waves at the moon, just in case.

On the calendar there is a big red circle. That's when Nana is coming to visit.

Every morning, {name} counts the days. Not long now.

title: A personal story for a toddler moving from a cot to a big bed
summary: A cosy story about moving from a cot to a big bed, and the bedtime routine that stays the same.
why_it_helps: Moving from a cot to a bed is a big step in independence, and it often brings bedtime battles. A story that keeps the familiar routine and makes the new bed exciting helps toddlers feel proud rather than unsettled.
tips:
Let them help choose the bedding if you can.
Keep every step of the bedtime routine the same as before.
Read the story in the new bed on the first night.
sample_story:
{name}'s cot is getting too small. {name}'s feet nearly touch the end!

"Time for a big bed," says Papa.

The big bed has a cover with stars on it. It's low down, so {name} can climb in all by {name}self.

Bedtime is the same as always. Bath. Pyjamas. Teeth. One story. Two cuddles. Night light on.

"Do I stay in my bed all night?" asks {name}.

"Yes," says Papa. "Big beds are for big sleeps. And I'll see you in the morning."

{name} snuggles under the stars. The bed is big and soft and warm.

In the morning, the sun peeks in. {name} sits up and smiles.

"I slept in my big bed!"

title: A personal story for a child whose pet has died
summary: A gentle, honest story to help a child remember a pet who has died and talk about missing them.
why_it_helps: Losing a pet is often a child's first experience of death. Clear, gentle words help more than euphemisms like 'went to sleep', which can confuse or frighten young children. A story full of real memories of their pet gives them a way to remember and to talk about how they feel, now and later.
tips:
Use your pet's real name and favourite habits.
Use clear words like 'died' rather than 'went away'.
Let your child add their own drawing of their pet to the last page.
sample_story:
Biscuit was {name}'s dog. He had one floppy ear and he loved chasing leaves.

Biscuit got very old and very poorly. One day, the vet told {name}'s family that Biscuit had died. His body had stopped working, and it couldn't start again.

{name} felt sad. Really, really sad. {name} cried, and Mum cried too. It's OK to cry when you miss someone.

That evening, they made a memory jar. {name} wrote: Biscuit chased leaves. Biscuit snored. Biscuit liked toast crusts.

Some days, {name} still feels sad about Biscuit. Some days {name} remembers him and smiles.

When the autumn leaves fall, {name} kicks them high, just like Biscuit used to chase them.

"That one's for you, Biscuit."
